blocks.text: Writers teach that among the Egyptian serpents the asps are by far the largest. Ammianus, book 22: Egypt also nourishes countless serpents, raging beyond all destructiveness: basilisks, amphisbaenas, and scytales, and acontias, and dipsades, and vipers, and many others; all of which the asp easily surpasses in size and beauty, and it never of its own accord leaves the streams of the Nile. Nicander assigns them a μῆκος [mēkos], a length, ὀργυῇ μετρητὸν [orgyē metrēton], measurable by the orgya (or ell). Strabo, following him, says in book 17: Διττὴ δ᾽ ἔστιν, ἡ μὲν σπιθαμιαῖα, ἥπερ καὶ ὀξυθανατωτέρα· ἥδ’ ἐγγὺς ὀργυιᾶς [Dittē d' estin, hē men spithamiaia, hēper kai oxythanatōtera; hēd' engys orgyias]. The asp is of two kinds: one a span long, which kills more quickly; the other nearly an orgyia. In Aelian, book 16, ch. 39, the Egyptians say ἀσπίδας τετραπήχεις γίνεσθαι πολλάκις [aspidas tetrapēcheis ginesthai pollakis], that asps are often four cubits long. And, on the same witness, book 6, chapter 38, γίνονται καὶ πενταπήχεις [ginontai kai pentapēcheis], there are also some of five cubits. In Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 1, ch. 21, three species of asps are reckoned: terrestrial, chelidonian and ptyades; of which the terrestrial [III, 159] are larger, and are sometimes found up to five cubits in length. Just so Avicenna says of the dry asp: هي في قدرها ما بين ثلثة اذرع الي خمسة اذرع [hiya fī qadrihā mā bayna thalathat adhruʿ ilā khamsat adhruʿ] In its size it is from three to five cubits. When serpents have reached this bulk, they begin to be called dragons. Hence Aëtius, in the chapter On Dragons: Some are five cubits, others ten; there are also some that extend to thirty cubits, and certain ones are even said to be larger. And Avicenna: اصغر اصناف الثنانين علي ما ذكره بعضهم خمسة اذرع واما الكبار فتكون [col. 383] من ثلثين ذراعا الي ما فوق ذلك [aṣghar aṣnāf al-thanānīn ʿalā mā dhakarahu baʿḍuhum khamsat adhruʿ wa-ammā al-kibār fa-takūn min thalāthīn dhirāʿan ilā mā fawqa dhālika] The smallest species of dragons, as some report, is five cubits; but the largest are thirty cubits and more. Since, then, asps grow to the bulk of dragons, it is not without reason that the Hebrew name פתן pethen was common to the dragon and the asp. Accordingly, for the gall of פתנים pethanim the Syriac has ܡܪܪܬܐ ܕܬܢܝܢܐ, and the Arabic مرارة التنين [marārat al-tinnīn], the gall of the dragon; and the Greeks θυμὸν δρακόντων [thymon drakontōn]. The former at Iob. XX, 14, the latter a little later at verse 16. I add that פתן pethen and תנין thanin (the common name of the dragon) are set as virtual synonyms in Psal. XCI, 13. and Deut. XXXII, 33. In the latter passage, for the plural פתנים pethanim, Jonathan has פיתוניא pithunja, as if from a singular פיתון pithun. And to this the Greek name PYTHON seems to allude, by which the poets call the dragon slain on Parnassus by Apollo. Yet Ephorus wrote that it was not a dragon but a man; from him Strabo, book 9, reports that Apollo killed with arrows χαλεπὸν ἄνδρα, Πύθωνα τοὔνομα, ἐπίκλησιν δὲ Δράκοντα [chalepon andra, Pythōna tounoma, epiklēsin de Drakonta], a savage man, Python by name, Dragon by surname, after he had long harassed the people of Parnassus with murders and robberies. The same figure is named Delphynes instead of Python by Suidas ^{a)} following Apollonius ^{b)}. If I see anything in this darkness, he was a notorious brigand in Phocis, whose real name was Delphynes. The surname Python was given him by the Phoenicians, then living in neighbouring Boeotia, because of the tumults he stirred up and the robberies he committed. For among the Arabs (with whom Phe stands in place of Pe, since they lack the letter Pe) فتن [fatana] phathana is to stir up tumults; فتنة [fitna] phithna, sedition, slaughter; فتان [fattān] phatthan, seditious, a robber, a highwayman. But this highwayman was turned into a dragon by the fabricators of fables, because among the Syrians ܦܬܢ pethen, or ܦܝܬܘܢ pithun, signifies a dragon. So he was also called Python. From this Python come the Pythian games; and the city of Delphi was called Πυθὼ [Pythō] or Πυθών [Pythōn], and Apollo himself Πύθων [Pythōn]. Macrobius, book 1, ch. 20: The Greeks tell the fable that this name (Πύθων [Pythōn]) was given to the god from the slaying of the dragon. Thus [III, 160] in Actor. XVI, 16. πνεῦμα Πύθωνος [pneuma Pythōnos] is the spirit of Apollo, the demon with which that ἐγγαστρίμυθος [engastrimythos] woman was believed to be filled. Hence ventriloquists themselves were formerly called Εὐρυκλέας [Eurykleas] and are now called Πύθωνας [Pythōnas], says Plutarch in the book On the Failure of Oracles. In this sense, for Python the Hebrews write פיתום Pithom, the word being slightly altered. And they dream that this kind of soothsayer uttered his voice not from the belly but from the armpits. The Talmudists in Sanhedrin, ch. 7, fol. 65a: בעל אוב זה פיתום המדבר משחיו, Baal Ob is the same as Pithom, that is, one who speaks from his armpits. And there the Gloss: מעלה את המת מן הארץ ומושיב לו בשחיו תחת זרועותיו ומדבר He brings up the dead from the earth, and sets him under his armpits and arms, so that he speaks. Accordingly R. Selomo on Deut. XVIII, 11., explaining what שואל אוב is, one who consults Ob (or a Python): זה מכשפות ששמו פיתום ומדבר משחיו ומעלה את המת בבית השחי שלו, This is the divination called pithom, by which one speaks from the armpits, calling up the dead to the place of the armpits. Whoever wants more on this rite should consult Maimonides in the treatise On Idolatry, at the very beginning of ch. 6. The author of the Aruch holds that פיתום Pithom is so called as if פי־תהום pi-thehom, mouth of the abyss. Rather, פיתום pithom and Πύθων [Pythōn] are the same, and both are formed from פתן pethen, [col. 384] or פיתון pethun, as we have said.
